body.heading: Green is chlorophyll’s colour
paragraphs: A summer leaf is green because it is packed with chlorophyll, the pigment that captures sunlight for photosynthesis. Chlorophyll is so strong a colour that it masks everything else in the leaf.

But the leaf was never only green. All summer long it also holds yellow and orange pigments called carotenoids — the same family of pigments that colours carrots. You just cannot see them under the green.

body.heading: The great reveal
paragraphs: As days shorten and nights cool, trees begin to withdraw from their leaves. Chlorophyll breaks down and is not replaced, the green drains away, and the yellows and oranges finally show through.

The reds and purples are a different story: many trees make those pigments, called anthocyanins, fresh in autumn. Scientists think they may act as a kind of sunscreen, protecting the leaf while the tree reclaims valuable nutrients from it.

body.heading: Why trees bother
paragraphs: Before a leaf falls, the tree salvages what it can — especially nitrogen and other nutrients that are costly to gather from the soil. The colour change is part of an orderly retreat.
Then the leaves drop, and the tree rests through winter with its savings banked in trunk and roots, ready for spring.

takeaway: Autumn colour is partly an unveiling: when green chlorophyll fades, the yellows and oranges that were always there shine through.
